Players deposit WLD tokens when they opt into a duel bracket (1 WLD, 10 WLD, or 100 WLD), and the tokens remain locked until a winner is determined. The Node.js backend tracks each player’s Wordle solution details—like the number of attempts, green blocks, and yellow blocks—and decides the winner once both participants have completed their puzzle. It then signs a signature given to the winner, so he can unlock his winnings from the escrow.

name: Watchtower
tagline: Atomic Liquidation and Other Actions via 1-time Hooks 4 Sale on Uniswap V4
prizes: Best Multi-chain App with Nodit's Web3 Data API
desc: Watchtower ,  a novel protocol for atomic price action triggered interventions. Uniswap V4 Hooks have allowed this protocol to react to price changes caused by executions of swaps. The reactions are atomic first-in-line without a possibility for anyone to intercept and front-run the reacting transaction. Watchtower allows for anyone to permissionlessly subscribe to desired price actions caused by swaps and and take advantage of the prompt atomic actions as desired. Such actions can be delinquent loan liquidations, limit orders, undercollateralized option and/or derivative liquidations and many other use cases. The implementation was facilitated by our One-time Hooks, which can be attached and detached dynamically to Uniswap V4 pools. Watchtower has an economic incentive model that is beneficial to all parties involved.
how: Pure Solidity to implement an elaborate Uniswap V4 hook that can manage dynamic "hooks". How does this work? In order to act on-chain, someone needs to initiate the contract call. This is not done by keepers, but by swap callers on Uniswap V4. Unknowingly they can cause action trigger calls, which does not cost them anything and they are rewarded for this as well. The user simply visits the Web3 front end of Uniswap V4. As soon as they ask for a swap, the Uniswap V4 calculates a route for the most efficient execution of the swap. Multiple pools can be used, but almost no pool is left behind, as if that happens, the pool in question remains behind with a more favorable price and it becomes even more attractive. This is achieved via an Uniswap V4 Hook, attached to one of the above described pools. This hook can be used by multiple pools, as many as one would want. However this hook is quite complicated. As Uniswap V4 hooks are permanently attached to the pools, this hook: Manages a data structure of registered Watch-ers ("hooks for sale"; not Uniswap hooks). These Watch-ers can execute one-time, pay for this to both the swapper and the pool and drop off. As the price moves, it performs the proper calculation to efficiently trigger the appropriate Watch-ers in constant time ($O(1)$). Cleans up to avoid storage cost and get storage refunds.
wins: Best Multi-chain App with Nodit's Web3 Data API | 2nd place

name: ED3N

desc: ED3N is a next-generation SocialFi platform that incentivises the hosting and attending of events via platform-native token staking. When a new user signs up, the metal.build API-based platform generates a custodial wallet for the new account. The platform native token can be earned/bought by users. Event hosts can set a threshold for native-token staking for their events. The higher the total stake, the higher-ranked and better-promoted the event. Attendees stake the native token to gain entry to events. If they don't show up, 100% of the staked platform is burned; if attendees do attend the event, then 45% of the staked token is distributed to the host, 45% is returned to the attendee, and 10% is burned. When sign-up is approved by the host, the platform auto-mints an NFT on Polygon and sends it to the user's custodial wallet, which contains an encrypted QR code (to prevent platform fraud) that acts as entry-ticket to the event. After the event, the NFT acts as commemorative memorabilia for attendance of that (and other prior) events.

name: VoucherToken

desc: Overall Architecture The system is built on an EVM-compatible blockchain and utilizes two token standards to meet its requirements: Merchant Certification: Uses the ERC721 standard to issue non-transferable certification tokens that record the merchant type and expiration time, ensuring that only qualified merchants can participate in voucher redemptions. Voucher Management: Based on the ERC1155 standard, it supports multiple voucher types. In addition, the system includes fund management functions that support deposits, withdrawals, and immediate payment during voucher redemption. Voucher Contract defineVoucherType: Defines a voucher type by setting its expiration, maximum usage count, single usage limit, and allowed merchant types. mintVoucher: Issues vouchers to a specified address; each address can only receive a voucher of a given type once. useVoucher: When a consumer uses a voucher, it verifies the validity of the
how: We built this project with two smart contracts using OpenZeppelin libraries—one ERC721 for non-transferable merchant certifications (by overriding the transfer update) and one ERC1155 for vouchers with expiry and usage limits. We used Hardhat with the MultiBaas plugin from Curvegrid to deploy on Celo and interact with the contracts via a REST API. On the frontend, Next.js, React, RainbowKit, wagmi, and Tailwind CSS were combined, with the MultiBaas SDK tying everything together for smooth blockchain interactions.

how: ZEST Protocol is a Bitcoin-native stablecoin ecosystem built on the Citrea network, combining Bitcoin’s security with Citrea’s EVM-compatible scalability. Our CI/CD pipeline is powered by GitHub Actions for clean and automated development workf

name: Just Pay
tagline: Just Pay sends USDC chainlessly in seconds—no bridges, one balance, one tap, any chain.
prizes: Build a Multichain USDC Payment System
desc: Just Pay is a chain-abstracted USDC payment app that turns complex multi-chain interactions into a one-tap experience. Users see one USDC balance and send payments without ever thinking about what chain they’re on. From the user’s perspective, USDC is chainless. Under the hood, Just Pay leverages Circle’s Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol V2 (CCTP V2) to move native USDC across chains using a secure burn-and-mint model backed by a global overcollateralization pool. One of Just Pay’s core innovations is its single-signature architecture: users authorize just one transaction, and the app handles all multi-chain coordination behind the scenes. No wallet pop-ups, no chain switching, no re-approvals. Key strengths: Chainless USDC Experience: Users interact with a unified USDC balance, no matter which chain their funds are on. Single-Signature Simplicity: Complex cross-chain transfers and aggregation logic are triggered with just one user signature. Fast, Secure Transfers: Transactions complete in seconds—even on slow-finality chains like Ethereum L1—via CCTP V2’s Fast Transfer mechanism. No Bridges or Wrapping: Just Pay uses native USDC only, avoiding common bridge-related risks. Just Pay abstracts away blockchain complexity entirely—bringing the security of native USDC and the performance of modern fintech into one unified experience.
how: We built Just Pay as a full-stack dApp to enable single-signature, chainless USDC transfers using @Circle’s CCTP V2. The frontend is built with Next.js, integrating RainbowKit and wagmi for wallet connectivity and signature handling. Our backend uses Node.js and MongoDB to manage session state and transfer coordination. Smart contracts are written in Solidity and developed with Hardhat. Just Pay leverages CCTP V2’s Fast Transfer and Iris API to perform near-instant native USDC transfers without bridges or wrapped tokens. We abstract away chain logic entirely—users see one balance, and everything else is handled under the hood. A particularly hacky and critical component is our custom signature mechanism. We designed a scheme that lets the user sign once for multi-chain operations, while embedding intent, function scope, expiration, and allowed chains into the payload. Each contract validates this context to prevent misuse or replay, enabling secure, cross-chain execution with a single signature. Using CCTP V2 gave us the speed, security, and composability needed to create a chainless payment experience that feels like modern fintech.
wins: Build a Multichain USDC Payment System

how: Our protocol enables seamless cross-chain gas payments using USDC, powered by Coinbase’s Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP). When a user initiates a transaction, USDC is sent across chains via CCTP. The protocol then automatically estimates the required gas on the destination chain and uses the received USDC to purchase just enough gas for execution. To support this mechanism, investors can provide capital and receive returns through our dividend-bearing token, "XFR". Profits generated from gas markups and usage fees are distributed to XFR holders.

name: fortun3.guru

It blends blockchain transparency, artificial intelligence, and the ancient tradition of fortune-telling to create a truly unique Web3 experience. At its core, Fortun3 allows users to exchange USDC for F3 tokens, which are then used to “consult the Prophet.” Users choose a source of destiny — their wallet address, a transaction hash, or a specific timestamp. Each of these inputs carries unique symbolic and data-driven meaning, which is then interpreted by a fine-tuned AI agent. Once a destiny source is selected and a prompt is submitted, the platform fetches relevant on-chain data using third-party APIs like Etherscan, BlockScout, and 1inch. This data is combined with user input and sent to the Prophet AI Agent, a language model configured to generate personalized, poetic, and often mystical readings. The result is returned to the user in text (and optionally, voice), and also minted as a Destiny NFT, permanently stored on IPFS. This not only gives users verifiable ownership of their prophecy, but also lets them collect and revisit their past readings through a Destiny Journal. Fortun3 is built for accessibility. Users exchange USDC for F3 tokens via the F3Token contract and initiate consultations by calling the pay() function in the CounterService contract. These interactions emit on-chain events, which are picked up by an off-chain Watcher service. This data, along with the user’s prompt, is sent to the Prophet AI Agent — a custom LLM interface powered by OpenAI or similar models — designed to generate symbolic, poetic horoscopes. name: Solva

desc: UX is well known to be one of the subject that need a lot of improvements in Web3 - there's just too much terms and concepts to understand for your mother to start using a web3 app. Solva (from the latin solvere, to settle / pay / solve) aims to be a user friendly replacement to a quick payment app like Venmo or PayPal, using crypto under the hood without you even knowing it. Create an account with your email or social login with Google/Apple etc, choose a username and you are ready to go! Top up your account with a credit card and send money to your friends & family in a few clicks without ever seeing a transaction signature modal or seeing the words "gas fees". If you are already a degen, you can of course login with your favorite wallet, top up your account with crypto on EVM chains, and take full control of your underlying wallet at any time (which Solva never has access to). Solva is a Real World payment app, for Real World users.
how: To provide a seamless experience, Solva leverages several technologies. The first one is the social login & account abstraction with gas sponsorship by Thirdweb to allow user to connect with familiar methods and interact like they would in a Web2 app. To abstract addresses, ENS subnames of solva-app.eth are used on Polygon mainnet. Interactions with the ENS smart contracts are done by our backend that uses a Cloud Wallet from Curvegrid for simplified blockchain interactions. End users just have to choose a username that isn't already used, and the corresponding ENS subname will be assigned to their address. They can also upload a profile picture, that will be uploaded & pinned on IPFS with Pinata, and saved in the avatar text record of the ENS. To transfer funds, a proxy smart contract (also on Polygon mainnet) is used to make some checks and emit an event for easy tracking. This event is send to the backend by a Curvegrid webhook to allow it to index transactions in a PostgreSQL database, used to easily and rapidly retrieve informations when a user navigates in the app (all the data in the database can be reconstituted from the on chain interactions). A potential business model would be to charge transaction fees on payments made to business, and although this wasn't implemented during the hackathon, advanced users can still create webhooks to be alerted on new incoming transactions, which could be one of the feature given to enterprise users.

desc: This project is a job-based incentive platform that uses smart contracts and decentralized identity tools to enable trusted, onchain task collaboration. When a job is about to be assigned, the system performs an on-demand verification of the job assigner using Self Protocol, specifically to check whether the assigner is subject to financial sanctions (e.g., OFAC lists). This verification helps the platform assess a risk score for each job, protecting users from interacting with high-risk or non-compliant parties. Each job has a reward locked in a smart contract escrow, ensuring funds are only released upon verified task completion. This reduces risk for both job assigners and doers. Key features: Sanction screening and risk scoring for job assigners before tasks are assigned. Decentralized identity integration via Self Protocol. Trustless reward flow via smart contract escrow. A secure, reputation-based ecosystem for onchain work. The result is a privacy-preserving, compliance-aware platform where users are empowered to work safely and get paid transparently.

Smart Contracts: Written in Solidity and deployed on the Celo Mainnet. The reward escrow contract ensures that funds are only released upon successful task completion and verification. Backend: For this hackathon version, we’re using a mock backend to simulate task listings and credential lookups. In the future, we plan to implement a full Node.js + Express backend to handle job assignment logic, Self Protocol integrations, and risk scoring computation. This allows the system to assign a risk score to each job and ensure compliance before escrow funds are locked. 🤯 Hacky Highlights: We implemented on-demand compliance checks instead of upfront verification to reduce friction and protect user privacy. name: Signals
tagline: More accurate, more rewarding. Financially incentivized BTC price predictions visualized as heat map
desc: Info finance is a field that “begins with the piece of information you want to uncover and deliberately designs a market to extract that information optimally.” Our platform uses probability-based dynamic pricing to go beyond observing market signals and transform crowd sentiment into concrete, quantitative insights. When multiple participants predict a specific price range for Bitcoin, the probability for that range increases, and corresponding movements in market prices result in a real-time market consensus. Users who make accurate predictions are rewarded from a shared pool, naturally encouraging precise forecasting and enhancing data quality. The information gathered in this process captures the market’s broader sentiment as an objective and reliable indicator, providing valuable insights for investment decisions, strategic planning, and beyond. By contrast, traditional prediction markets often rely on binary (“yes/no”) outcomes, which can be limiting when trying to forecast continuous values like asset prices. Our platform addresses this limitation through a multi-outcome structure that lets users predict specific BTC price ranges, drawing out more refined, detailed insights from the crowd. As a result, we move beyond a simple “will it go up or down?” model, achieving segmented market consensus in real time, incentivizing accurate predictions through a rewarding system, and ultimately turning crowd sentiment into meaningful quantitative insights.
how: Architecture & Pricing Method 1-1. Interval-Based Forecasting ✔️ The BTC price range is segmented into clearly defined intervals (e.g., $80,000–$81,000, $81,000–$82,000). ✔️ Users can easily select and purchase tickets (shares) for one or multiple intervals, simplifying the prediction process. 1-2. Probability Density-Based Pricing ✔️ Similar to how Polymarket assigns an 80-cent price to a 1-share purchase for an event assessed at 80% probability, our system prices tickets according to the probability density within each interval. ✔️ While Polymarket utilizes an order book structure, matching buy and sell orders directly, we implement our proprietary Automated Market Maker (AMM). This AMM model dynamically adjusts prices upward as participation in a specific interval increases, ensuring that the expected payout for tickets ultimately equals $1. On-Chain Price Verification & Daily Settlement 2-1. Daily On-Chain Price Verification ✔️ Every day, the platform retrieves the closing BTC price from decentralized on-chain sources (e.g., Uniswap), providing transparent and trustworthy daily price confirmations. 2-2. Reward Claims ✔️ When the actual daily closing price falls within a specific interval, ticket holders for that interval can initiate transactions to claim their rewards. Features & Advantages 3-1. Multiple Intervals in One Transaction ✔️ Users can conveniently select multiple intervals simultaneously, allowing easy, detailed forecasting. 3-2. Dynamic Probability Pricing ✔️

IntelliGuard was born to bridge this gap, empowering users with an intelligent, proactive defense against crypto hacks. By leveraging AI to analyze transactions in real-time, IntelliGuard aims to prevent losses, build trust in DeFi, and make Web3 safer for everyone—from casual traders to seasoned degens. how: Hoja is a food ordering app that incorporates blockchain technology to enhance the payment and review process. The app allows users to verify if today is their birthday using Self Protocol. If it is, users are eligible for a birthday discount. After verifying the birthday, users can proceed with payment via Polygon or Celo blockchain networks, offering low-cost and fast transactions. Once the payment is completed, the app adds the user to a Semaphore group and generates a ZK Proof to ensure privacy. With this proof, users can then leave anonymous reviews on the app. Here’s how we built it: Self Protocol Integration: We integrated Self Protocol to verify users' birthday information. name: OniBlock
tagline: Uniswap v4 hook where an AI prices toxic arbitrage every block, and loses power if it's wrong.
desc: Oniblock is a Uniswap v4 hook that protects liquidity providers from toxic arbitrage without making ordinary traders pay for it. The problem. When ETH moves on Binance, a Uniswap pool's price is briefly stale. Arbitrageurs buy the cheap side and LPs absorb the loss. On Ethereum this adds up to hundreds of millions of dollars in CEX–DEX arbitrage over the past two years. Private mempools protect traders from sandwiches, but they do nothing for LPs, because the arbitrage trade itself is the problem. Fixed fees and fixed thresholds are walls: they either tax everyone or let arbitrage through. How it works. Every block, an AI decides how sensitive the fee should be. A keeper sends the pool's state to Jev, TypeSafe's typed decision model, and asks two questions in one call: How likely is it that the next block brings flow that costs LPs money? What kind is it: CEX–DEX arbitrage, split arbitrage, backrun, JIT liquidity, sandwich, or none? The state it sends is the Binance mid vs the pool price, the arbitrage edge at the base fee, flow imbalance, trade size vs depth, volatility, and recent liquidity churn. The keeper signs the answer with EIP-712 and posts it on-chain. The contract turns that answer into two bounded knobs. k, the fee sensitivity, is 0.8 × p × confidence. Only swaps that move the pool toward Binance (the arbitrage direction) pay fee = 0.30% + k × live gap, capped at 1%. Everyone else pays the base fee. The JIT penalty window runs from 10 to 100 blocks. Liquidity remo
how: Architecture. Four pieces: a Uniswap v4 hook (Solidity, Foundry), a keeper and settler (TypeScript, viem), an ENSv2 setup, and a Next.js app. Everything runs on Ethereum Sepolia against the real v4 PoolManager and the ENSv2 Sepolia contracts. The hook (OniblockHook.sol). Dynamic fee: beforeSwap returns fee | OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG. The fee is computed only from on-chain state: the pool price vs the last attested Binance mid, and the attested k. Contracts can't call a model, so the model's opinion is pushed in beforehand as a signed attestation, and beforeSwap only reads it. Directional: only swaps that move the pool toward the mid pay the gap premium. Split-arb resistant: a per-block high-water anchor makes a split arbitrage pay the first sub-swap's fee on every part. Never reverts in the swap path: a stale oracle falls back to a conservative fee, and all data checks happen in the keeper's setAttestation transaction. beforeSwap hands the fee to afterSwap through transient storage, which emits a Receipt event with every input. JIT: built on OpenZeppelin's LiquidityPenaltyHook, with two changes: The penalty window is set by the model per block, and each position is judged by the window in force when it was added. When the last LP exits inside the window we park the penalty as ERC-6909 claims instead of reverting, so withdrawals never brick. Calibration gate: k comes from the model only while its node is allowlisted and its on-chain Brier score is under 0.25. Tests: 146 Foundry tests

name: Radius
tagline: Radius makes your ENS subname the credential for every piece of infrastructure in a network
prizes: Best Integration of ENSv2 into an Existing Project
desc: Most networks — corporate offices, university campuses, co-working spaces, event venues — still run on shared passwords, manual key distribution, and flat access for everyone. There's no per-person policy, no isolation between roles, no audit trail, no revocation without a full credential reset. Identity is an afterthought bolted on after the fact, if at all. Radius is an identity-gated network and API access control system. Any organization with an ENS name can use it — a company, a university, an event venue. Your ENS subname becomes the sole credential for everything: WiFi admission, bandwidth tier, sponsor or internal API access, SSH. The subname carries your role, your access policy, and your device group in ENS text records. The infrastructure reads ENS instead of a password database. No VPN client, no RADIUS server, no manual provisioning — mint a subname, walk in, connect. The system enforces access in three layers: a captive portal gates WiFi entry and assigns per-role bandwidth tiers at the kernel level, a resource proxy intercepts every API call and injects keys server-side so credentials are never exposed to end users, and an operator console lets administrators define groups, set per-identity and per-group daily quotas, rotate keys atomically, and revoke sessions in real time. Every admission, every proxied request, every quota check is logged against a session identity — not a bare IP — giving operators the first real audit trail without a dedicated security app
how: 1. Mint at check-in. Every attendee gets a subname under the event domain — philo.tokyo2026.ethglobal.eth . The organizer writes their role, bandwidth policy, SSH public key, and device group directly into ENS text records. No database entry. No password issued. The subname is the credential. 2. Captive portal reads ENS, not a password DB. When a device connects to the event WiFi, it hits the captive portal. The attendee signs an EIP-191 challenge with their wallet. The portal resolves the signing address to an ENS subname, reads the wifi-tier and wifi-bandwidth records, and maps them to an access group. That's the only auth check. 3. Network enforcement runs at the kernel level. Login triggers two things instantly: an iptables rule marks the device's traffic with an fwmark tied to its tier, and a tc HTB class enforces bandwidth — 5 Mbit for basic attendees, 10 Mbit for staff, 1 Gbit for VIP. Cross-tier FORWARD DROP rules prevent devices on different tiers from reaching each other at all. Device isolation is structural, not policy — there's nothing to misconfigure. 4. A resource proxy injects API keys server-side. All sponsor API access goes through a proxy layer. Attendees never see the keys. The proxy reads the active session, checks group membership and daily usage counters, then forwards the request with the key injected — into the URL path, query param, or header depending on the upstream. name: Kagi Wallet
tagline: Give AI agents delegated keys from a self-custody MPC wallet. Spend more? Your ESP32s sign over IR.
desc: Kagi is an open-source threshold wallet for AI agents. It gives your agent its own spending key, capped and set to expire, while the key that actually controls your money stays split across hardware you hold. Agents need money to be useful, but today you pick between two bad options. Either you give the agent a hot key, and one prompt injection drains you, or you approve every transaction, and the agent is useless. Most crypto theft comes down to a stolen key, so we made sure no single device, server or phone ever holds one. Kagi splits every key with FROST threshold Schnorr signatures (the RFC 9591 family), and each half is useless on its own. Together they produce one standard BIP340 signature. Kagi works as a spending ladder: Under the cap: your agent pays on its own with an ephemeral session key. The smart account enforces the limit and the expiry on-chain, so the agent can't overspend even if it's compromised. Over the cap: the agent files an on-chain request with its reason. Your phone shows it, and you approve with your fingerprint plus a held button on your Kagi Wallet, an off-the-shelf $21.50 ESP32 stick. Together they form a 2-of-2 key. The treasury: needs a 3-of-3 key that includes a second stick, the vault. After setup the vault keeps its radio off and signs only over infrared, so you have to walk over and point your Kagi Wallet at it. Revoke: hold the revoke button on the phone, or hold B on the stick for 2 seconds. Any AI can use it. ChatGPT, Claude, Claude Code
how: Hardware We used two M5Stack StickS3 boards (ESP32-S3), each with a screen, two buttons, a speaker and an IR transmitter and receiver. We flash the same firmware build to both, and a role saved on the device makes one stick the Kagi Wallet and the other the vault. The Kagi Wallet talks to the phone over Bluetooth LE. The vault joins the key once: we reshare it from 2-of-2 to 3-of-3 during a 2-minute radio window you open by holding a button on the vault. After that its radio stays off, and it signs only over infrared, after a press on the vault itself. We wrote the IR link ourselves on the ESP32's RMT peripheral: a 38 kHz carrier, NEC-style pulses, 4-byte frames with a sequence number, a CRC-8 and an acknowledgement, and retries, so a hand passing over the window slows a signature down instead of breaking it. Firmware The firmware is C++ built with PlatformIO. We wrote FROST ourselves on top of mbedTLS's big-number and elliptic-curve primitives, and used NimBLE for Bluetooth and M5Unified for the display, buttons and speaker. The IR link talks to the ESP32's RMT peripheral directly through ESP-IDF. Every approval is a deliberate hold on the button, and letting go early cancels it. The speaker stays quiet while the IR receiver is listening, because the StickS3 can't do both at once. Smart contracts The contracts are Solidity 0.8.30, built with Foundry. name: Wamia
tagline: A liquidity backstop for yield trading that stops unfair liquidations.
desc: Wamia is a standing liquidity backstop for Pendle's PT (yield trading) markets, built for 1inch's "Build an Aqua App" track. On Aug 25, 2026, an attacker forced Pendle's router to sell millions of PT reUSD by repeatedly buying YT, pushing PT price down about 3% in roughly 9 minutes. Morpho's 15 minute TWAP oracle followed that dip down, and borrowers who had done nothing wrong got liquidated. $37.35M in debt became eligible for liquidation across 20 positions, even though PT's actual value at maturity never changed. Wamia addresses this by giving the market a bid that's always there. LPs ship idle capital (SY, Pendle's yield bearing wrapper token) to a Wamia strategy on 1inch Aqua, without locking it up. The strategy runs a pricing algorithm that reads live onchain Pendle, Curve and SY state on every trade and decides whether the current PT price looks like manipulation or a genuine repricing. When it judges a dip to be manipulation, it pays a small discount to fair value for PT; when the signals look more like a real depeg, a real loss in the vault's rate, or a real news driven move, the algorithm scales its discount down or stops quoting rather than absorbing the loss. When someone dumps PT into a thin pool and Wamia is willing to buy, a zero capital searcher sells that PT to Wamia and immediately buys it back on Pendle in the same transaction, helping pull the price back up before the oracle average can drag it down further. In a fork replay of the real attack, 5M SY of Wa
how: Wamia runs entirely on 1inch's deployed, unmodified contracts: Aqua v1.0.0 and AquaSwapVMRouter (swap-vm v1.0.2). A Wamia strategy is a SwapVM order whose program is a single Extruction instruction pointing at WamiaQuoter, a stateless Solidity contract that prices every PT sale from maker-set parameters and live onchain reads: Pendle's spot, the SY exchange rate, and Curve's reUSD/USDC EMA price, never from taker-supplied data. Two optional v2 steps, WamiaRateGuard and WamiaSpendLimit, compose into the same program to add a high-water-mark check and a per-block spend cap. WamiaArb is the zero-capital searcher contract: it sells PT to Wamia through the router, and inside the router's preTransferInCallback immediately buys that PT back on Pendle with the SY it just received, keeping the leftover PT as profit or reverting if unprofitable. The contracts are built and tested in Foundry, with unit tests, a full local deployment of real Aqua/SwapVM release tags, and fork tests against live Pendle, Morpho and Curve contracts at the exact block of the Aug 25 attack. On the TypeScript side, @1inch/aqua-sdk and @1inch/swap-vm-sdk build the same order and program that the Solidity side produces, verified byte-for-byte (including the strategy hash) by a dedicated parity test. Fork replays use viem and anvil to mine block-by-block against forked mainnet state, comparing no-backstop, a reactive taker bot, and Wamia at several capital levels. name: Surety
tagline: Insurance for AI agents you trust with money: if one gets tricked, you're paid back the same day
prizes: Best Use of World ID for Agents
desc: Surety is parametric, on-chain insurance for AI agents that handle money. The problem: AI agents now hold wallets and pay, trade and settle on people's behalf. When one is manipulated, the loss has no backstop. In May 2026 a single Morse-coded message tricked Grok's Bankr agent into sending roughly $150–200K. If you use a company's trading or payments agent and it gets tricked, no product covers you, and standard insurance policies have started excluding AI losses (the ISO endorsements from Jan 1, 2026). Worse, the agent's own signature proves nothing, because the agent's key is exactly what gets compromised. What Surety does: enforce where you can, insure what gets through. The policy is an ENS name. Buying cover mints a non-transferable ENSv2 subname such as payments2.surety.eth, with its own PermissionedResolver. Its text records are the rules: per-transaction cap, counterparty allowlist, coverage, tier and status, so anyone can read and verify them. Enhanced Access Control lets the agent's key update only its own "streak" record. The rules are enforced by a Uniswap v4 hook. The agent spends from an AgentVault. Every swap goes through our SuretyHook, whose beforeSwap reverts any trade over the cap or to a counterparty not on the allowlist, before any money moves. Violations are recorded and recomputable. Plain transfers can't be blocked, so they're recorded. A ViolationOracle recomputes "over the cap" or "off the allowlist" from public data alone. There's no adjuster and n

SuretyHook is our Uniswap v4 hook: it enforces the rules and holds the claims reserve.      - ViolationOracle recomputes bre WorldIdGate verifies EIP-712 approvals and IDKit humans.                                    - ClaimRouter handles file → verling checks. PricingEngine is the credibility-weighted premium formula.                                  - PremiumYieldVault turns part oidity for backers. The suite has 135 Foundry tests,variant tests and a real-Sepoliafork suite that registers real ENSv2 names and swaps through the real PoolManager. ENS (ENSv2, Sepolia beta). We registered surety.eth through the ETHRegistrar (commit/reveal), with a UserRegistry deployed viaregistry. Each policy is anon-transferable subname. We found that Enhanced Access Control scopes permissions to         (resolver, key), so with a sharek" permission would leak to every other policy. name: Relay
tagline: Bundle your APIs then delegate by ENS name to anyone with Enhanced Access Control
desc: Relay explores a simpler way to share API access across an organization: bundle all the API and delegate the API permissions through ENSv2 Enhanced Access Control. As we start to adopt AI agents, access becomes harder to manage. Employees, agents, and subagents need different services, spending allowances, and session durations. Sharing a single credential makes it difficult to track responsibility or withdraw access from one branch. Relay organizes these relationships into six levels: company → department → team → user → agent → subagent. An interactive access tree shows each identity, its provider permissions, and its relationship to the rest of the organization. Names such as derek.eng.sodalabs.eth make the delegation path readable. Children entity can only access API services their parents allow with and simulated usage counts toward every ancestor’s allowance. An integrated activity log makes changes visible alongside the tree. Our goal is to let organizations delegate API access with only 1 API without distributing the underlying API.
how: Relay is built with Next.js App Router, React, JavaScript, and custom CSS. The page layout and dashboard are React components, while an interaction controller manages tree selection, department filtering, zoom, provider lists, permission editing, and activity updates. The permission model is separated from the interface in a JavaScript module. Each identity stores its parent, wallet address, provider allowances, budget period, usage, and optional expiry. The model walks the ancestor chain to calculate inherited access and the remaining allowance. Before accepting simulated usage, it checks the entire chain, then updates each ancestor’s usage so multiple descendants consume a shared parent budget. Revocation and expiry also propagate through that chain. The access tree uses positioned cards and SVG connections. A fit-to-view calculation scales the hierarchy to its container. Provider marks are inline SVGs sourced from Simple Icons and Lobe Icons, restyled into a consistent khaki-and-stone badge system. Overflow circles reveal the complete provider list without crowding the cards. One practical implementation choice was to preserve the original DOM-based interaction controller during the Next.js migration, mounting it through a React effect with cleanup for listeners, timers, and observers. This let us retain the prototype’s interactions while separating the permission logic for testing. Automated tests use Node’s built-in test runner to cover hierarchy construction, permission

name: XSwap
tagline: One-click Uniswap buys from X cashtags, with scam checks and World ID-verified creator kickbacks
prizes: Add Payment Screening to Your Agent or x402 Service
desc: XSwap is a Chrome extension that lets you buy a token right from the place you find it: a tweet on X. When a tweet mentions a supported cashtag like $ETH, $UNI or $AERO, X shows a ticker card. XSwap adds a Buy button to that card. Pressing it opens a swap panel inside the card, so you never leave your timeline, open a DEX in another tab or copy-paste a contract address. You pick an amount, get a live quote, and sign the swap with your own browser wallet (e.g. MetaMask). These are real onchain swaps with real funds. How it works Uniswap swaps: quotes and swaps run through the Uniswap Trading API on Base, Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism and Unichain. The extension never holds your keys. Your wallet signs every transaction. Token safety with Intercepta: buying straight from a tweet is exactly where people get scammed. So before you buy, XSwap checks both the token and the swap transaction with Intercepta. Risky tokens get a warning or are blocked outright, and you must confirm before you can continue. Creator kickbacks with World ID: the author of a tweet earns 0.5% of every buy made from the ticker card in their tweet, paid straight to their wallet through Uniswap's integrator fee. This rewards the people whose calls actually drive volume. That reward would invite farming with many X accounts, so authors must first prove with World ID (Proof of Human) that they're a unique human. The backend verifies the proof and stores the nullifier, so one human can earn on only one X account.
how: XSwap has two parts: a Chrome extension (Manifest V3, plain JavaScript, no build step) and a small Node/Express backend. The backend proxies every partner API, so the Uniswap and Intercepta keys and the World ID signing key never ship in the extension. The extension A content script watches the X timeline for tweets that contain a ticker card and adds a Buy button to each one. The swap panel is rendered in a Shadow DOM, so X's styles and ours don't clash. It reads X's own colors, so it looks native in light, dim and dark mode. Content scripts can't access window.ethereum, so we inject a small bridge script into the page that relays wallet requests and events over postMessage. That way MetaMask or any other injected wallet works without leaving X. Partner technologies Uniswap Trading API: the panel runs the full check_approval → quote → swap flow on Base, Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism and Unichain, with Permit2 signatures where needed. We map each cashtag to the right token on each chain (e.g. $BTC is cbBTC on Base, WBTC elsewhere). It gave us good routing across five chains without deploying a contract. Its integratorFees option is also how creator kickbacks are paid, inside the same swap. Intercepta: before a buy we fetch the token's risk verdict (block, warn or info, with reasons), and we simulate the actual swap transaction too. Verdicts are cached on the backend so scrolling past cards doesn't burn credits. Buying straight from a tweet is where people get scammed, so this

name: AntiScalper Protocol
tagline: Sybil-resistant access to scarce physical drops: World ID gates the claim, Sui settles it.
desc: AntiScalper Protocol (ASP) is an access-control and payment layer for physical machines, designed to prevent scalping on limited releases. Payment on its own proves that a transaction happened, not who made it or whether they already claimed. Scalpers exploit that gap by opening more wallets. Asp closes it by combining two primitives: World ID (Proof of Human) binds each entitlement to a unique human through a zero-knowledge nullifier. Sui handles settlement. Machines can be hired programmatically over x402, and at the point of sale the buyer pays through Sui Payment Kit (Slush). Claim flow: Registration: the user verifies with World ID and receives a ticket bound to their nullifier. Authorization: at the kiosk, the user re-verifies. The claim is authorized only if the nullifier matches the ticket holder and the proof is bound to that specific claim request. Settlement: the kiosk issues a Payment Kit request as a Slush QR code. The gateway confirms the on-chain PaymentReceipt before continuing. Fulfillment: the gateway sends a single dispense command over MQTT to an ESP32-controlled motor. Each entitlement can be redeemed exactly once. Replayed proofs, mismatched identities, and repeat claims are rejected before payment or dispense. Machines stay hireable over x402, but a PoH-gated release cannot be purchased without World verification. Live demo: https://altaga-asp.expo.app
how: World ID integration: IDKit 4.0 with Selfie Check. RP signatures are generated server-side, so the signing key never reaches the client. Every proof is verified against World's /api/v4/verify endpoint. Authorization fails closed; client-side success callbacks are never trusted on their own. The claim signal is set to the claim request ID, so each proof is bound to a single claim and cannot be replayed. The gateway enforces a strict nullifier-to-ticket mapping: one human, one ticket, one redemption. Sui integration: x402: POST /asp/hire returns an HTTP 402 challenge, built on @altaga/x402-sui exact-payment schemes with sponsored gas. Apps and agents can hire machine capabilities programmatically. Payment Kit: the gateway builds Payment Kit transaction URIs (receiver, amount, USDC, nonce) and exposes them as Slush deep links. Settlement is confirmed by matching the PaymentReceipt event on-chain by nonce, amount, and receiver. Both payment paths go through the same policy check (assertHireAllowed), so PoH-gated capabilities cannot be bought without prior World authorization.

name: Tide
tagline: A Partially Active AMM that hides most of its inventory from arbitrage bots every block.
desc: Every constant-product pool leaks money to arbitrage: the first trader of each block is a bot that trades the whole pool to the new price, and liquidity providers pay for it. Uniswap LPs lose an estimated several hundred million dollars a year this way, which is why passive liquidity keeps thinning out. Tide is a partially active AMM (PA-AMM) built on the recent "activeness" research. Each block it exposes only a fraction λ of a maker's inventory to the first trade, so the bot reaches a slice instead of the vault. Every later trade in the block is quoted on a curve N times deeper, inside a tight drift band δ, so ordinary traders get better prices than the plain pool while the maker's loss to arbitrage drops by a third at λ = 0.5. A flat fee backs the deep curve; the contracts enforce (N − 1)·δ ≤ 2·fee, so the deep curve can never be farmed. For a deeper dive, please check out the whitepaper at https://tide-amm.vercel.app/WHITEPAPER.pdf For LPs it is a strategy layer: you name it on ENS, choose how much to show per block, ship, and keep custody. A manager agent watches realised volatility and retunes λ, N and δ on its own inside guardrails you set on-chain; anything outside them needs your fresh World ID sign-in and your wallet. Traders get a routing terminal that quotes every live Tide strategy and fills through the best one. Live on Sepolia: two venues sharing one math library, five public strategies, reusable templates, a whitepaper with the proofs, and 54 tests. The busine
how: One Solidity library, TideMath, holds the active split, the N-scaled quote, the drift guard, the solvency bound and the fee arithmetic. It is checked against a Python reference on 24 vectors and imported by two venues, so a cross-venue test asserts identical fills: 1inch Aqua. Tide is a SwapVM program of three custom opcodes in unallocated slots (ACTIVE_SPLIT, VIRTUAL_XYC, BUFFER_GUARD) on a redeployed router from the hackathon template. Each opcode scans the program and reverts unless the three appear once, in order, so nothing can jump around the guard. The maker's tokens never leave the wallet; Aqua pulls at fill time. A TideTaker contract builds taker traits on-chain so a wallet can quote and fill in one call. SwapVM has no block hook, so the re-split is lazy: it runs inside the first quote of a new block and is persisted by the first fill. Uniswap v4. The same steps inside beforeSwap of a BaseCustomCurve hook returning a BeforeSwapDelta for the whole amount, reserves as ERC-6909 claims, pro-rata shares, and liquidity changes refused in any block that already saw a swap. The hook claims its pool id in TideParams at initialize, so nobody can squat a predictable key. ENS v2 on Sepolia. Each strategy is a subname of tide.eth whose text records are the parameters; nothing is hard-coded. The manager agent has its own name, manager.tide.eth, with a resolver role scoped to exactly the lambda, N and delta records, revocable per record. TideParams mirrors the records on-chain with

name: Placed
tagline: A global ad market for attention: auction ad space anywhere, on anything, and trade future revenue.
desc: In an AI-slop world, human attention is the scarcest resource. Placed is a global marketplace for attention, that connects advertising space with brands and investors. Anyone can list an ad-space they control (eg. clothing, X-banner, billboard space etc.) and make it discoverable to brands worldwide. Open auctions let brands worldwide bid on ad space, helping owners discover what it’s worth and earn from advertisers beyond their existing audience or local market. Placed makes small, unconventional sponsorships easier to discover, compare and book. Space owners upload photos, define ad slots on their space through interactive 3D models, and auction ads slots for defined periods. Brands discover spaces, preview their ads on the models, and bid to book campaigns. A portion of the winning bid stays in escrow subject to release upon verification of campaign completion by AI image verification. For spaces with recurring advertising potential, space owners can raise capital by tokenizing a share of their space's future advertising income. Investors purchase and trade revenue-share ad-space tokens through Uniswap CCA, creatomg price discovery for future revenue claims. Advertisement payments are split between the space-owner and the tokenholders’. Placed connects scarce advertising opportunities with global demand: helping creators earn more from the surfaces they control, brands find novel ways to get noticed, and investors access sponsorship revenue.
how: Placed runs on Ethereum Sepolia, with a Next.js, React and TypeScript frontend. Its Three.js studio lets creators import or generate models through Meshy, position sponsor artwork on surfaces, and publish those placements as listings. Privy handles wallets, Viem manages contract interactions. Space-owners list advertising space, and brands bid for it in USDC. A smart contract holds bids, lets outbid brands withdraw their funds, and releases payments as the campaign is fulfilled. Uniswap — fundraising, price discovery and trading. Space-owners can optionally launch a fixed-supply ERC-20 representing a defined share of an asset’s advertising revenue over a fixed term. CCA distributes tokens and discovers their initial price. Successful launches use the Liquidity Launchpad strategy to allocate reserved tokens and part of the proceeds to a v4 trading pool, with available remaining proceeds paid to the creator. World ID — limiting duplicate-account abuse. IDKit provides human-verification proofs that the backend validates and binds to participant wallets. This makes duplicate-account spam and self-bidding through multiple wallets harder, without collecting legal names. It verifies participant uniqueness, not asset ownership or fulfillment. ENSv2 — identifiable inventory and controlled artwork updates. Assets and ad slots receive consistent names linking to metadata, artwork and revenue-token references. Dedicated slot resolvers let winning advertisers update only their own placeme

name: VexiHakari
tagline: Options via 1inch Aqua, with tokens pulled at fill and a Uniswap v4 TWAP quote guard.
prizes: Build an Aqua App - Continuity Track
desc: Writing a fully collateralised option today means locking the collateral in a protocol before anyone buys. The LPs with the most depth will not hand over custody, so option books stay thin. VexiHakari turns 1inch Aqua into an options vault. An AquaVault is a shared vault whose own address is the Aqua maker: anyone deposits AAPL and USDG for shares, and the vault ships that one balance, as virtual balances, to two strategies at once. The first is an AquaWriter, an Aqua app that posts covered calls and cash-secured puts across a whole board of strikes and expiries. Posting moves nothing; when a buyer buys, Aqua pulls exactly the collateral of the contracts sold, inside the buyer's transaction, and at a buyback or at expiry Aqua pushes it home into the same strategy. The second is a SwapVM spot pool on the same balance, optionally concentrated with XYCConcentrate, which earns spot fees while the options wait. The two must not sell the same token twice. ExposureGuard, a custom SwapVM instruction, shrinks the spot pool to what open option orders have not promised, at the same price, so a buyer who sees option depth can always fill it. It runs as an opcode on our router and, through SwapVM's Extruction, on 1inch's already-deployed router with no redeploy. DeltaSkew, a second instruction, leans the spot price against the delta the option book added. In the trading app, every option is priced when it trades, never stored: VaultPricer computes Black-Scholes from the spot of the vault'
how: The project has two Foundry packages. The oracle hook uses Solidity 0.8.26 with Uniswap v4-core and OpenZeppelin uniswap-hooks. The Aqua integration uses Solidity 0.8.30 with Cancun and via-IR, pinned 1inch Aqua and SwapVM dependencies, OpenZeppelin Contracts and Uniswap v4 libraries. AquaWriter connects OptionBook to Aqua. During a purchase, the book checks the quote and available collateral, invokes Aqua.pull through the writer, and verifies the exact token balance increase. Return and premium-claim operations use Aqua.push. The maker's virtual balances, wallet balance and allowance all affect what can actually fill. ExposureGuard is a custom SwapVM instruction that caps spot depth at unpromised inventory without changing the quoted price. We demonstrate it both on our router extension and through Extruction on the canonical deployed router. The latter lets the guard execute without replacing 1inch's existing router. HakariOracleHook adds a combined raw/truncated TWAP view to OpenZeppelin's BaseOracleHook. StabilityBandPricer reads pool state through StateLibrary and observations through the pool's hook, then enforces the fixed-width demonstration band, per-call size taper and spread adjustment. FixedPremium supplies expiring demonstration quotes with optional original-price anchors. HookTwapExpiryPrice is a separate experimental settlement-window adapter. name: Bailiff
tagline: Any keeper can liquidate restricted-RWA loans via Uniswap v4. The RWA never leaves the allowlist.
desc: Restricted RWA tokens (ERC-3643 style) only move to wallets the issuer has allowlisted. On lending markets like Aave Horizon, seized RWA collateral can only go to the issuer's allowlisted holders. So liquidators must be KYC'd, pre-funded in stablecoins and able to hold the RWA. If that small group is slow or missing, lenders can be left with bad debt. Bailiff splits the trigger from the receiver. Any keeper can call the LiquidationAdapter, even with 0 USDC. In one transaction it sells the seized RWA on a Uniswap v4 permissioned pool, repays the liquidated debt and pays the keeper a USDC bounty. The keeper never touches the RWA. If the sale cannot cover the debt, everything reverts. Bailiff expands the keeper set without expanding the holder set. The issuer keeps control. On the liquidation side it flags one sell-only contract, the adapter, next to the pool's own wrapper, and never the keeper. The token's controls (allowlist, freeze, pause, forced transfer) and the issuer's bounded NAV oracle still apply. Revoke the adapter and the same keeper call reverts in Uniswap's hook. Bailiff is an extra route next to KYC liquidators, not a replacement. The buyer is the pool's allowlisted LP, a KYC market maker in the demo, whose USDC sits in the pool ahead of time. Aave's liquidationCall sends the collateral first and pulls the stablecoin from the caller at the end, with no callback in between. v4 flash accounting lets the adapter sell the RWA before it holds it, so the keeper fronts n

The demo runs on an Anvil fork of Sepolia and the pinned tests on a Foundry fork, both at block 11782723, against Uniswap Labs' deployed PoolManager, PermissionsAdapterFactory and PermissionedHooks. My PermissionsAdapter comes from the real factory, and the adapter's constructor checks verifiedPermissionsAdapterOf. Inside one PoolManager.unlock, LiquidationAdapter: previews the exact repay and seize amounts swaps exactly the seize amount of vRWA (the PermissionsAdapter wrapper) for USDC. Flash accounting leaves the vRWA delta open, so it sells collateral it does not hold yet. No keeper capital, no flash loan. before any transfer: reverts if proceeds < repay; bounty = min(surplus * keeperBps / 10,000, the market's 6% bonus on repay); reverts if bounty < minBounty takes the USDC, repays the market, receives the RWA closes the vRWA delta: sync, RWA to the PermissionsAdapter, wrapToPoolManager, settle pays the keeper and pushes the rest to the borrower Notes: msgSender() returns the adapter, so Uniswap's hook checks the adapter, not the keeper. PermissionedV4Router checks allowedHooks and the deployed hook leaves that to callers. The adapter calls PoolManager directly, so it runs the same check (test_adapter_hookNotAllowed). MockRWA3643 (ERC-3643-style: HOLDER, freeze, pause, forcedTransfer; no ONCHAINID) is its own IAllowlistChecker. One issuer registry answers Uniswap's SWAP/LIQUIDITY flags and the

name: Takarabako
tagline: Takarabako helps turn your leftover travel cash into dollar savings
prizes: Build an Aqua App - Continuity Track
desc: Leftover travel cash becomes dollar savings. Every trip ends the same way: a few foreign banknotes in your pocket. Too little to be worth exchanging, too much to throw away, and useless once you're home. Takarabako (宝箱, "treasure box" in Japanese) gives that cash somewhere to go. HOW IT WORKS FOR A TRAVELER Sign up with just an email. You get a wallet without a seed phrase or an app, plus a personal ENS name like alice-1a2b.takarabako.eth. For example, at the Takarabako kiosk in Tokyo, scan your QR code and feed in your banknotes. Each note is converted at the live exchange rate and becomes a US-dollar balance on Ethereum, which earns a small base yield. You watch a lacquered treasure box on screen fill with gold as each deposit confirms. You don't need to know anything about crypto: the kiosk does the work, and your cash keeps its value after you fly home. For every dollar deposited you also receive tkCASH, a token worth one US dollar of the banknotes inside that specific machine. tkCASH is created only when a note goes in and destroyed when cash comes out, so the total supply always matches the cash the kiosks hold. WHY YOU CAN TRUST THE MACHINE The kiosk is a verifiable machine. Its ENS name, tokyo-01.takarabako.eth, publishes the key it signs every note with, and that key was generated on the device itself. A deposit only counts if the signature matches the kiosk's name, so a fake box or a replayed signature can't create money. Every receipt shows "✓ tokyo-01.takarabako.e
how: Takarabako has four parts: a physical kiosk, a Node/TypeScript backend, a Next.js 16 web app, and five Solidity contracts on Ethereum Sepolia (all verified on Etherscan). THE KIOSK (HARDWARE) A Raspberry Pi 4 with a touchscreen drives a TB74 bill acceptor on its serial port (ICT protocol, 9600 8E1). A Python listener accepts a note only while a customer is logged in. Otherwise it refuses the note and the acceptor hands it back. It also reports unrecognized notes so the screen can tell the customer to try again. A small Node bridge on the Pi turns each accepted note into a deposit and signs it with a key generated on the Pi itself (EIP-712 NoteAccepted: kiosk, amount, currency, session, nonce, time). The Python code never sees account IDs or talks to the backend directly. CONTRACTS (Solidity, Foundry) TakarabakoVault: an ERC-4626-style vault holding each customer's USDC balance, with a base APY that accrues over time. TakarabakoCashReceipt (tkCASH): the cash in the box as a token. The treasury mints it in recordCashIn and burns it in redeem, updating that kiosk's on-chain reserve each time, so supply always equals total reserves. We fuzz-test this in Foundry. attestReserve records an operator's physical count and freezes the kiosk on any mismatch. Transfers between holders require both wallets to be allowlisted, stay under a $500/day limit, and stop when the contract is paused. Minting and burning skip those rules, so redemption is never blocked. Mock USDC and mock ETH (testne
