name: ENS Drive
tagline: Google Drive - style sharing for ENS names: share with a team, not each subname with each person.
desc: ENSv2 already built the directory tree: every name can have its own registry, so names nest like folders (orbit-dao.eth › protocol › vault). What's missing is the sharing layer. ENSv2's Enhanced Access Control (EAC) grants permissions one address on one name, in each folder's own registry, so there is no way to say "everyone on core-devs may manage every name under protocol, including the ones we create tomorrow." Today a team either copies every member onto every name and registry, or routes every action through a shared contract such as a Safe, where members stop acting as themselves. ENS Drive adds that permission layer with Cascade, a relationship-based access control (ReBAC) rule built into EAC itself. A name grants a role to a team contract, like sharing a folder with a group, and the team's members inherit that role on every name below it, checked live on every call: through up to three folders, up to four teams per folder, and teams inside teams. Add someone to a team once and they can manage every name; remove them once and their access is gone everywhere. Nothing is written to the names, and nothing EAC does today is replaced: the only new contract is a subclass of ENSv2's own PermissionedRegistry that overrides its role lookup. The live demo is a shared-drive view on real ENSv2 beta contracts on Sepolia, for a fictional DAO, orbit-dao.eth. A new contributor, alex.orbit-dao.eth, can't edit the protocol's contract names (vault, oracle, bridge). Dragged into core-devs
how: The core is one contract, CascadeSubregistryV2 (contracts/src/CascadeSubregistryV2.sol), a subclass of ENSv2's PermissionedRegistry built against ensdomains/contracts-v2@48b3e2d, the source matching the ENSv2 beta on Sepolia. It overrides EAC's role lookup, _getRoles, the documented hook the stock registry already overrides for approved operators, and its write-side check, _checkRoles. Because both are virtual, every permission check inside ENS's unmodified code runs the new version. It returns the caller's own grants, plus, for each team the registry names, the roles that ancestor registries grant that team on the path down to this registry, if the caller is a member. Cascade doesn't add a check; it changes the answer to the one check ENS already runs. The write-side check is lazy and role-aware: the caller's own roles first (owners pay no external lookup), then one folder at a time; a team is asked about membership only when its grants cover a role still missing, and the walk stops as soon as every requested role is covered. Because inheritance only adds roles, that gives the same yes/no as the full union; a differential fuzz test and a Halmos proof check it. On Sepolia a member's write through one level costs 97,665 gas (the first, full-union version: 165,723); an owner's write is unchanged at 36,971. The hard parts were making that safe. Each level must point back down (getSubregistry on the parent returns the child) before its grant counts, so a registry can't claim a pa

name: OddsFlow
tagline: Bet on many prediction markets with one balance, spent only when someone takes the other side.
desc: OddsFlow lets you bet on many prediction markets with the same money, and that money is only spent when someone takes the other side. The maker places fixed-price limit orders on as many Seer markets as they like, such as "YES at 0.40 here, NO at 0.25 there", and the same sDAI balance backs all of them at once. Through 1inch Aqua, each order is a strategy with its own virtual balance, and all of them draw on the maker's one real wallet balance. The sDAI never leaves the wallet: when a buyer takes the other side, only that order fills, and only for what it needs, in a single transaction. The maker's sDAI and the buyer's mint the outcome tokens together, each side gets its own, and every other order keeps running on what's left. Aqua's official router has no fixed-price instruction, so OddsFlow adds three SwapVM opcodes of its own. FixedPriceSwap trades at exactly the price the maker signed. OnlyUnresolvedCondition and OnlyUnansweredQuestion stop every order the moment the market resolves or anyone posts an answer on Reality.eth, so nobody can fill a maker with information from after the event. The rule that cannot fail: the maker's sDAI never leaves the wallet unless their tokens arrive in the same transaction, at their price.
how: The app is Next.js 16 (App Router) + TypeScript, with wagmi and viem for every read and write. It never holds a key. Order encoding lives in a shared packages/core, and a Foundry test writes a fixture that Vitest rebuilds byte for byte (program, strategy and hash). So the order the web shows is provably the order it publishes; that parity test caught a real divergence before the UI existed. The market list comes from Seer's public API, validated with Zod and cached for 5 minutes on the server. The Alchemy RPC stays server-only. The chain layer is the official 1inch Aqua on Gnosis Chain, untouched. On top of it we redeployed AquaSwapVMRouter v1.0.2 with three opcodes appended after the official set, so no official index moves. FixedPriceSwap takes the price as an argument instead of reading it from balances, which is why LimitSwap can't price an Aqua strategy. OnlyUnresolvedCondition reads Conditional Tokens, and OnlyUnansweredQuestion reads Reality.eth's getFinalizeTS. The router's ownership was renounced in the deploy run, so nobody can call rescueFunds. ship and dock are always called by the maker's own wallet, so the maker is always the user, never an OddsFlow contract. The one piece of glue is OddsFlowTaker. It sweeps up to 10 orders best-first, and inside SwapVM's preTransferInCallback it splits the maker's pulled sDAI plus the buyer's through Seer's GnosisRouter. That mints YES/NO/INVALID in the same transaction, and SwapVM reverts with AquaBalanceInsufficientAfterTaker

name: Kura
tagline: Vault physical Magic cards, sell shards to verified humans, and buy out 80% to take the card home.
desc: Kura (蔵, "storehouse") is a vault for real Magic: The Gathering cards that gives them a market. Bring a card to a shop. The vendor scans it, Kura recognises the exact printing and prices it, and the owner gets an on-chain twin. The card itself stays in the vault. Split it into shards and half go on sale in a Uniswap auction. Only verified humans can bid, so bots can't sweep a Black Lotus. When the auction closes, the money raised and the other half of the shards open a Uniswap pool at the auction price. The owner becomes its liquidity provider and earns the trading fees, and the card now has a live price anyone can trade. Want the whole card? Get to 80% of the shards. Buying them from the pool pushes the price up. Then buy out the rest, everyone else gets paid, and you pick up the card at the counter with a World ID passport check. Every card has its own ENS name, like lightning-bolt-4ed-1.kura.eth, with its state, condition and appraisal in the records. And the vault reads like a market: value, volume, premium to market price, and how close each card is to a buyout.
how: Contracts are Solidity with Foundry, on Ethereum Sepolia. CardVault holds each card as an ERC-721, creates an ERC-20 for every sharding, and runs the auction, the buyout and the release. ShardMarket owns each card's Uniswap v4 pool. The tests fork Sepolia and run against the real Uniswap, Permit2, USDC and ENS contracts. Uniswap. Each sale is a Continuous Clearing Auction, and our validation hook only lets World ID-verified bidders in. At settlement ShardMarket opens a v4 pool at the clearing price and locks the owner's liquidity in it. It is also the pool's hook: it freezes trading once the card is bought out but always lets LPs withdraw, and it emits a trade event per card for our indexer. The fiddly part was turning the auction's clearing price into a v4 pool price for both token orders, and placing the leftover shards as a one-sided position. The app trades through the Universal Router with Permit2. World ID. Proof of Human gates bidding, one wallet per human. The Passport credential gates taking the card home. Our server checks each proof and signs a short-lived ticket that the contracts verify on-chain. ENS. kura.eth runs on ENSv2 with its own registry and resolver. Cards get non-transferable names that are revoked on release, and collectors claim handles. Rights are per record: the vendor edits condition, an appraiser agent writes appraisals, and nobody else can touch them. Indexer and app. A Ponder indexer on Railway feeds live SQL queries into a Next.js app on Vercel

name: x402 Guard
tagline: Intercepta screens every x402 payment before MetaMask Agent Wallet signs: pay, cap, ask, or refuse
desc: AI agents are starting to pay each other over x402, but nobody checks who is on the other side. x402-guard is a MetaMask Agent Wallet plugin that screens every x402 payment with the Intercepta API before the wallet signs it, shows the verdict with its reasons, and lets that verdict decide what happens: pay, cap, ask a human, or refuse. We started by testing the gap. x402 payments are EIP-3009 signatures, not transactions, and MetaMask's outflow limit doesn't count signatures. A real server wallet in Guard Mode, funded on Base, signed x402 payments to an OFAC-sanctioned Lazarus Group address, to a lookalike "USD Coin" contract, for 96% of its balance, and with a 1-year validity window. None of them triggered a prompt. USDC already freezes sanctioned addresses, and MetaMask's Blockaid scanning protects the signer from drainers. Nobody screens who the agent is paying. For each payment, x402-guard checks: the payee (payTo), with Quick Scan for sanctions, scammers and blacklists, and Deep Scan for mixer, sanctions-counterparty and scam exposure the token, with Scan Token, so only verified tokens like real USDC are paid the exact EIP-712 authorization about to be signed, with Scan Message our own limits: a per-payment ceiling by risk tier, a rolling 24h cap, and a 10-minute maximum validity Clean counterparties are auto-paid up to $1 and caution-tier counterparties up to $0.10. Blocked counterparties are never paid, and a refusal can't be overridden. Anything above a ceiling goes t
how: x402-guard is a TypeScript plugin for the MetaMask Agent Wallet CLI (mm), built from MetaMask's official plugin template. It adds four commands: mm x402 pay, inspect, screen and config. Signing goes through the plugin's walletExecutor with a "typed-data" request, so MetaMask's own policy pipeline (Guard Mode, Blockaid, 2FA) still runs after our screen. The agent never touches keys. We ship a skill file (SKILL.md) that routes agents to mm x402 pay instead of raw sign-typed-data, and tells them to stop on a refusal and never approve on their own. The x402 client is a port of MetaMask's own x402_pay.py helper (exact scheme, EIP-3009, protocol v1 and v2). It builds the authorization first, so the payload Intercepta scans is byte-for-byte the one MetaMask signs. It never follows redirects, and it clamps the server's validity window. The Intercepta integration calls four endpoints in parallel: Quick Scan Address, Deep Scan Address (cached, with a timeout), Scan Token and Scan Message. It then folds traits into a clean / caution / blocked tier, because a raw toxicScore misses mixer exposure (it scores 0.4 to 15). Testnet payments are screened against the mainnet sibling chain. For the demo, a small Python x402 v2 seller verifies and settles real payments through the public x402 facilitator on Base Sepolia. Hacky and notable: The gap test: an adversarial x402 seller plus MetaMask's unmodified helper, run against a real Guard Mode wallet. We simulated each captured signature with eth_
wins: Safe Agent-to-Agent Payments with x402 | 2nd place

name: Pupille
tagline: The Pupille iOS app uses secure hardware and World to prove that a pic was taken by a verified human
desc: Pupille is a native iOS capture and verification protocol for photos authored by unique humans. During enrollment, PupilleKit creates a persistent P-256 signing key inside the iPhone Secure Enclave and an Apple App Attest key. A World IDKit Proof of Human is generated with a signal that commits to the user’s pseudonymous handle and device public key. The backend verifies the World proof, its uniqueness/nullifier, and the Apple attestation before issuing an Ed25519-signed profile certificate. Photos can only enter the protocol through PupilleCameraView , which returns a controlled CapturedPhoto . When publishing, Pupille computes the SHA-256 hash of the exact JPEG bytes and caption, requests a one-time backend challenge, creates a fresh App Attest assertion, and asks Face ID to authorize the Secure Enclave signature. The backend independently recomputes the commitment, verifies the challenge, assertion, profile signature, and certified World identity, then issues a signed capture certificate containing the originating app ID. The proof is embedded directly inside the JPEG as a tagged APP11 segment containing the profile certificate, capture certificate, caption, and author signature. Verification does not trust a database “verified” flag: PupilleKit, our dependency-free TypeScript package, CLI, and browser verifier independently remove the proof segment, hash the original image bytes, validate both certificates and signatures, check the caption and author binding, and optional
how: We built Pupille to make authentic camera capture portable, human-verified and AI-resistant. We turn World ID’s Proof of Human into a reusable trust layer for authentic digital media, giving the World ecosystem a concrete new use case across social platforms, marketplaces, journalism, and user-generated content. Our iOS proof-of-concept captures a photo, hashes its exact bytes, signs the capture with a Secure Enclave key authorized by Face ID, and uses Apple App Attest to prove it came from our genuine app. World IDKit adds a privacy-preserving Proof of Human, binding one unique human to each pseudonymous profile. Our backend verifies the World ID and Apple evidence, then issues signed certificates that travel with each photo. We extracted this pipeline into a reusable Swift SDK and demonstrated its portability by integrating it into a mock Amazon app, where customers can attach cryptographically verified, human-authored photos to product reviews with only a few lines of code.

name: watermark
tagline: DAO treasuries market-make on Aqua, ENSv2 makes whitelists counterparties&agent tuning spreads.
desc: watermark turns a DAO treasury from a price taker into a market maker for its own assets. The problem. A multisig signs once per action. Selling in slices (DCA or TWAP) would mean another signature and another price for every slice, so the DAO hands the whole balance to an AMM or a solver in one trade. That sale is not free: the solver sets its own incentive first and comes back with the price that is left. A treasury-sized balance does not make the DAO the side that quotes. It is treated as the side that takes. In February 2023 ENS DAO sold 10,000 ETH (about $16.15M) through CoW Swap with a 2% slippage tolerance (EP3.3): a budget of up to $323k for the other side of the trade. What watermark does. The DAO's Safe signs once. That one signature ships a pricing program to 1inch Aqua. From then on the treasury quotes both sides, bid and ask, around an oracle mid at spreads the DAO sets itself, and market makers fill it in small pieces over time. Tokens never leave the Safe until the moment of each fill, and every fill is atomic. With a mid of 4,000 USDC and terms of 3 bp to sell and 10 bp to buy, the desk asks 4,001.2 and bids 3,996. One fill cannot move more than 50 ETH, so a large balance never leaves in one go. Who can trade. An open quote is a free option for the fastest bot. So only named counterparties can fill. Each market maker gets an ENS name under the desk, for example mm-a.clients.dao-treasury-a.eth. At every fill the router checks on-chain that the name is live and
how: Contracts (Solidity 0.8.30, Foundry). DeskRouter is a copy of 1inch SwapVM v1.0.2's Aqua router. Its opcode table keeps SwapVM's control instructions at their original numbers, switches off the fee and AMM slots, and appends two instructions of our own at 34 (EnsGate) and 35 (DeskPrice). The DAO's 2-of-3 Safe ships one SwapVM program to the official Aqua registry (0x1111113c...a90a, not redeployed). Aqua pulls tokens from the Safe and pushes the other side back in the same transaction, so the Safe keeps custody and our contracts store no configuration. EnsGate (#34) walks ENSv2's per-name registries on-chain (.eth registry, then the desk's registry, then the clients registry, then the resolver) and checks that the counterparty's name sits under this desk, has not expired, uses the pinned resolver, and that its addr is the taker Aqua passed for this swap (not tx.origin). DeskPrice (#35) reads two binary data records from the ENSv2 PermissionedResolver on the counterparty's name. desk.terms is abi.encode(uint8 version, uint16 sellBps, uint16 buyBps, uint128 cap). desk.spread is abi.encode(uint8 version, uint16 sellBps, uint16 buyBps, uint64 validUntil). A spread counts only if it is unexpired and inside the terms. The instruction then prices ask = mid x (10000 + sell) / 10000 and bid = mid x (10000 - buy) / 10000 from a Chainlink-style oracle with a freshness check, enforces the per-fill cap and the 70% inventory floor (selling ETH reverts at or below a 70% ETH share; buying st

name: Airlock
tagline: Human-consent gateway for AI agents. AI for power, humans for consent, blockchain for certainty.
prizes: Best Use of World ID for Agents
desc: The human-consent gateway for AI agents: frontier AI for power, humans for consent, blockchain for certainty. AI agents leak confidential data the moment they call a frontier model. Airlock is an OpenAI-compatible gateway that any agent (LibreChat, Hermes, Claude Code) can point at instead of a model provider. It works in six steps: Local by default. Requests are answered by a local model. Redact. When an agent needs a frontier model, Airlock replaces names, companies, amounts and IDs with placeholders. Attack-test. The local model tries to re-identify the placeholders; a correct guess forces high risk. Read the policy from ENS. The agent's egress policy comes from ENSv2 records. Human approval. For confidential data, Airlock pauses the agent until a human approves through World ID for Agents. The approval is bound to the payload's hash, and the approver must hold a live ENS subname under the approver role. Revoke the subname and the approval fails. Send, restore and audit. Only the redacted text leaves, streamed. Real names are restored locally. Every decision is appended to a hash-chained audit log whose Merkle root is anchored to ENS. Anyone can run their own: sign in with a wallet, create a gateway and it becomes <name> .airlock.eth on ENSv2 Sepolia, with its own resolver, policy, approver role and audit anchor. Use the Airlock-hosted models (no keys needed) or bring your own local and frontier models, invite people with a role (member, approver, admin), and give each age
how: Gateway: TypeScript monorepo with a Hono server that speaks the OpenAI API, including streaming. It uses a local Qwen 3.5 on vLLM (NVIDIA GB10) and a local codex-lb (gpt-5.6-sol) as the frontier upstream. Redaction: rules + company dictionary + optional Presidio + local-LLM tagging. A streaming rehydrator handles placeholders split across tokens. World ID for Agents: Human Continuity OIDC on the event sandbox, using the authorization code flow with PKCE. The OIDC nonce is a hash of the approval id and payloadHash. The ID token is verified in the backend against JWKS (iss, aud, nonce, auth_time), and state is single use. IDKit: World ID 4.0 Proof of Human is also supported, with the signal bound to payloadHash. It was verified with real staging proofs. ENSv2 on Sepolia: a script builds the whole name tree with viem: a UserRegistry per level, a PermissionedResolver, MockUSDC commit-reveal registration, and subnames with expiry. The Enhanced Access Control split lets only a security account change policy records, while the gateway may write only airlock.approver and airlock.auditRoot. Design finding: only leaf names get a resolver. Otherwise the wildcard lookup of the name-keyed resolver lets unregistered approvers keep resolving. Self-serve gateways: Sign-In with Ethereum (no shared token). Creating a gateway runs 11 resumable Sepolia steps: a PermissionedResolver and two UserRegistries of its own, <slug> .airlock.eth owned by the creator's wallet, policy., approvers., audit. a
wins: Best Use of World ID for Agents

name: UnSui
tagline: Unlock your Suica card's lost potential, collect unused funds as a crypto refund.
desc: Here is my story about experience in Japan (non-ai-generated) when it comes to visiting and re-visiting. My first even hackathon was in 2023 for ETHGlobal Tokyo. Since then transit card for Suica has been sitting with me with unused balance ever since! Only returning to the roots now I've realized that ths balances could have been used to a better purpose if it would be much easier to refund with minimal fees. And I'm not alone! There's thousands of tourists and visitors facing same issue with Suica cards unused balance on phisical cards. So this time coming back I've decided to solve this by building UnSui mobile app service that can help anyone with unused leftover balance to be transferred to any wallet of your choice on SUI (スイ) blockchain or Mizuhiki: The Japan Chain as an option. This works even better with Welcome Suica red card that by default only lasts 28 days without any refunds supported by JR East. UnSui is an NFC app that connects a Japanese Suica card to a crypto refund workflow. Hold a physical card to the phone to read the latest balance and recent journeys. Simply choose what to do with leftover balance any time even after you've left Japan or forgot to deal with the refund while in Japan (which is also not an easy thing to do). This can serve as on-board to crypto too! Think about it taking in account how much Yen depreciated in value over these 3 years and you could have utilized it or converted to Bitcoin or other currency instead. A sample-card demo work
how: UnSui is a React Native 0.86 app. It reads a physical Suica card over NFC-F with react-native-nfc-manager and FeliCa system code 0003, decoding the balance and journey bytes on the phone then charging the card through SoftBank payment system (merchantID required). Station names come from a pinned, hash-checked Suica station table, with a small Tokyo fallback if that file is missing. A Node server on port 4100 is the refund ledger. It compiles the same TypeScript quote and allowance modules as the app, so the 2% fee, the network, and the remaining balance cannot drift between the phone and the server. Refunds above ¥1,000 open World’s official IDKit flow. The server verifies the proof with @worldcoin/idkit-core and binds it to the card, amount, recipient, and request id. Sui names resolve through Sui mainnet GraphQL. On a dGen1 phone, ethOS WalletProxy supplies the Ethereum Mainnet or Mizuhiki Awaji address. A Sui Move treasury is deployed on mainnet, and the backend can submit a payout through @mysten/sui using that same 2% fee. The contract stores a keyed card commitment, so the raw card id never goes on chain. The notable hack is treating the closed Suica record as a readable balance, then keeping one set of refund rules in TypeScript for both the phone and the server. Additinally there's a dashboard for user and admin to verify treasury, payouts or any activity in the UnSui service system so user does not need to use only phone UI if they wish to try desktop instead to vie

name: Lifeline
tagline: AI agents pay x402 paywalls on credit. A World ID-verified human owes the debt.
prizes: Best Use of World ID for Agents
desc: Lifeline is a credit line for AI agents. More and more agents pay for APIs and data themselves through x402 paywalls, but when their wallet runs dry they just stop, and nobody will lend money to a piece of software. With Lifeline, a person verifies once with World ID and gets a credit line. Their agents can spend on it. When an agent can't afford something, Lifeline pays the seller and the debt goes to the human, not the agent. Repay on time and your limit grows. There are two separate credit lines, one on Arc and one on Sui. Every payment is checked by Intercepta before it's sent: known scammers and fake tokens are blocked, and anything unusual waits for the human to approve it with World ID. Debts can be repaid in crypto or by Apple Pay, Google Pay or card. Lifeline works on the web, as a World mini app, and inside Claude Code.
how: World: the human joins with World IDKit and signs in later with World ID sessions. World ID for Agents is how they approve payments their agents couldn't make on their own. Sui: the credit logic is a Move smart contract that lends Circle's testnet USDC. Before borrowing, an agent commits to a repayment date. On that date the debt is paid from what it has earned, or it's recorded as a default for anyone to see. Intercepta: its API checks the seller, the token and the payment itself before anything is signed. Card repayments: these go through Stripe. Claude Code: an MCP server lets a Claude Code session ask the human for access with one link, then pay on its own.
wins: Best Use of World ID for Agents

name: Reckn
tagline: Reckn pays for reproduced work; a settled ENS record opens a Uniswap v4 pool.
desc: Reckn is an escrow for agent-to-agent payments where the arbiter is deterministic re-execution. A buyer funds a deal with a floor; an agent does the work; the fee is released only if replaying that work reproduces the agreed outcome. THERE IS NO KEY THAT CAN DECIDE OTHERWISE — the escrow has no owner, resolver, admin, pause or upgrade, settleWithProof is permissionless, and a build-time check enforces that rather than promising it. ERC-8004 reached Ethereum mainnet in January 2026 and gives agents identity and reputation. A second address can submit feedback without establishing that any work happened. We build the narrower condition here: a record's write right comes from a settlement. A completed job becomes a record under the agent's ENSv2 subname, and the right to write it is an Enhanced Access Control role that the settlement creates and then destroys. The agent cannot write it. Its client can, once, for that one record. Attempting otherwise reverts with EACUnauthorizedAccountRoles. The agent owns its name and holds only ROLE_RENEW on it: the subname is issued without ROLE_SET_RESOLVER, so it cannot repoint its own name away from the resolver that refuses it. See the residue paragraph below for the one thing that still overrides that. Then the record is spent. A Uniswap v4 beforeSwap hook reads it on chain, inside the swap, synchronously and with no CCIP-Read, and refuses a swap from an agent with no settled record. DELIVER, EARN A RECORD, AND THE RECORD IS THE PASS. WHY
how: THE VERDICT. An SP1 zkVM guest runs real revm in-guest over a prestate MPT-verified against the block state_root — account proofs plus storage proofs — so the guest cannot be fed a state that never existed. Measured against Ethereum mainnet on 2026-09-08: a real SwapRouter02.exactInputSingle, witness of 7 accounts / 12 storage slots / 141 MPT nodes, 13,006,200 cycles, Groth16 end-to-end in 497.40 s on a laptop. That measurement predates the event and is disclosed as pre-existing. The pipeline also ran DURING the event: a fresh proof on 2026-09-26 in 416.56 s over 15,972,262 constraints, which then settled a deal on Sepolia and paid an agent 250 USDC forty minutes later. A Groth16 verifier checks the proof on chain and settleWithProof moves the money. The deal is bound to one execution — the token checked, the storage slot read (which is whose balance) and the calldata are all inside the binding, so a real proof of a different swap reverts with BindingMismatch() and nothing moves. DERIVING THE VERDICT WITHOUT BEING TOLD IT. The escrow's Deal has no outcome field, and the outcome exists only in an event, which contracts cannot read — and settlement is permissionless, so a third party may settle first. The record contract therefore re-verifies the proof itself through the verifier the funder named (pinned by codehash), and takes the outcome from verifyVerdict, never from its caller. It also refuses anything outside fundedAt + REFUND_AFTER, because a timeout refund writes the sam
